memo
The memory and the process of a project built with agents

A command-line tool and a local web page over one store per repository; a skill or brief for each role an agent plays; and drains that work the queue unattended, each task in its own checkout.

Problem — without memo

Agents forget everything between sessions, and do what is cheapest rather than what they are told:

P1A fresh session rediscovers the code and guesses at past decisions.1 P2The developer is asked how code should work, and not what the product should do.9 P3An agent takes the cheapest path to whatever "done" is checked: it narrows the task and dismisses what review finds.4 7 P4Telling an agent how to behave changes nothing; a required output or a failing check does.11 P5An agent copies the nearest code, so copies of a rule drift apart.10 P6Several agents working at once trip over each other.5
Solution — with memo

The repository keeps what is true now; memo keeps what happened and why.

Done is an acceptance test, written in planning before the implementer starts. Fresh agents review and check, and the implementer fixes every confirmed defect and dismisses none.

Human attention is the scarcest resource. A project is healthy when only product questions reach the developer and escaped defects trend down.

Your attention goes here, and only here
  1. Planning with the tech lead: you judge what each task will do, never its code.
  2. Product questions, batched in the inbox, answered in a word.
  3. A retrospective: patterns across runs, as a handful of decisions.
  4. Curation: confirming where each recurring lesson goes.
  5. A defect you notice: traced to the task, run and step that let it through.

3 · Askyou answerWhat the software should do, look like or cover, with options, a lean, and before-and-after output or images. The answer requeues the task, and a principle in it joins the standard.

1 · RetrymemoA usage limit or a logged-out tool is retried, and a drain stops on a failure every task would share.
General notes — what memo asks of a project
  1. A check command runs every check, and a black-box suite drives the built product from outside. Landing runs it.
  2. A glossary of domain words and a standard of principles, both checked in. The tech lead, reviewer and debt survey use them.
  3. Prototypes checked in, where every run can see them. A page's look.
  4. No fixed ports and no state outside a checkout, so runs can go in parallel. Drains run side by side.
  5. Guidance that runs may edit; a check refuses any widened permission. Drains improve guidance too.

TECH LEAD

The tech lead does its own discovery, decides the order and scope of the tasks, and brings the how already decided. It asks you only what the software should do, and applies a principle you have stated before rather than asking again.

TASKS

A story carries its contract and its acceptance test. A bug carries its reproduction, run in planning, and its class with the search behind it. A refactor names a rule, its home to be and its copies, in domain words. memo refuses a task that lacks what its kind requires.

IMPLEMENT

Before any code, the implementer lists each rule the change computes and where it is computed today, and builds on that home. It works until the acceptance test and the check command pass. It may widen the task, with a reason; it may not narrow it, or touch the acceptance test.

REVIEW

A fresh reviewer, given the task and the diff and nothing of the implementer's reasoning, backs each finding with a failing test, and searches the code the change reads for other instances of its class. There are two rounds.

CHECK

A fresh checker runs each finding's evidence and judges only whether the defect is real, never whether it is worth fixing. A confirmed finding binds the run: the implementer fixes it and cannot dismiss it. Last, the checker confirms each fix by the reviewer's own test.

ACCEPTANCE

memo runs the task's acceptance test against main: a story's behaviour must be missing, and a bug must reproduce. If main moved and only the setup broke, the rebaser repairs the setup and may not change an assertion. A bug whose test passes on main asks you "already fixed?".
